syllabusTopics: Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes): preparation from haloalkanes (reduction and Wurtz reaction), decarboxylation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkene and alkyne
Chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration and sulphonation only), oxidation of ethane
Unsaturated hydrocarbons (Alkenes): preparation by dehydration of alcohol, dehydrohalogenation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkyne
Chemical properties of alkenes: addition reaction with HX (Markovnikov's addition and peroxide effect), H2O, O3, H2SO4 only
Alkynes: preparation from carbon and hydrogen, 1,2-dibromoethane, chloroform/iodoform only
Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes

rows.text: "Alkynes are prepared from calcium carbide and water, by double dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides, and by dehalogenation of haloforms with hot silver."

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Two π Bonds, One Carbon Rod Alkynes (**CₙH₂ₙ₋₂**) carry a C≡C triple bond. The syllabus routes to them start from the **elements themselves** (carbon + hydrogen → ethyne via calcium carbide) and from **vicinal dihalides** (1,2-dibromoethane) and **haloform-derived** substrates (chloroform/iodoform routes).  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 From carbon and hydrogen — industrial ethyne - **CaO + 3C → CaC₂ + CO** (electric furnace, ~2000 °C) — calcium carbide. - **CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)₂** — ethyne (acetylene) on contact with water. - Impure carbide gives PH₃/H₂S contamination — purified through acid or CuCl/NH₃ washes. ### 2.2 From 1,2-dibromoethane (vicinal dihalide) - **BrCH₂CH₂Br + 2 alc.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Carbide: two equations (furnace + hydrolysis). Vicinal dihalide: 2 alc. KOH, vinyl halide intermediate. Haloform + hot Ag: 2AgX by-products. Ethyne = acetylene = C2H2.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: A triple bond costs two eliminations: the first is easy (alkene formation), the second strips HX off an sp² carbon and demands a stronger base — difficulty rises with s-character.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Alkynes CnH2n-2, sp, C≡C. Preparation: (1) from elements: CaO + 3C -> CaC2 + CO (electric furnace ~2000C); CaC2 + 2H2O -> HCCH + Ca(OH)2 (industrial ethyne; impure gas washed of PH3/H2S). (2) From 1,2-dibromoethane (vicinal dihalide): BrCH2CH2Br + 2 alc.…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Ethyne burns at ~3300 °C in oxygen — the oxy-acetylene torch cuts steel, all from limestone, coke and water.

rows.text: ## 3. Scientific Definitions | Term | Scientific meaning | Example | |---|---|---| | **Calcium carbide route** | C + CaO → CaC₂, then hydrolysis to ethyne | CaC₂ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ | | **Vicinal dihalide** | Two halogens on adjacent carbons; double elimination gives the alkyne | 1,2-dibromoethane → ethyne | | **Vinyl halide** | Haloalkene intermediate of the first elimination |…  ·  ## 4. Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Why two eliminations are needed - A triple bond needs two π bonds; the first elimination makes the alkene (vinyl halide), the second must remove HX from an **sp² carbon** — harder, hence the stronger base (NaNH₂) for the second step in modern practice. ### 4.2 The carbide chemistry - CaC₂ is an **acetylide salt**: C₂²⁻ + 2H₂O → C₂H₂ + 2OH⁻.…  ·  ## 5. Comparison Tables **Three routes to alkynes** | Route | Starting material | Reagents | Product | |---|---|---|---| | carbide | CaO + C (electric furnace) | then H₂O | HC≡CH | | vicinal dihalide | BrCH₂CH₂Br | 2 alc. KOH (or NaNH₂) | HC≡CH | | haloform/Ag | CHCl₃ or CHI₃ | hot Ag powder | HC≡CH + 2AgX |
